A number of sources report that the Russian Armed Forces have deployed modernized Tunguska-M1 air defense systems on the front line. In particular, a rare 2S6M1 combat vehicle equipped with the latest digital optoelectronic and thermal imaging module from NPC "ELINS" has been spotted in the Dobropillia direction.

This modernization is designed to adapt the proven Soviet platform to combat small low-flying drones and barrage munitions.

The new sensor system provides the Tunguska-M1 with the ability to passively detect and track targets around the clock. This allows the crew to hunt down drones without turning on the radar. Stealth in the electromagnetic spectrum is critical for the survival of the system, as it protects the vehicle from enemy radio reconnaissance and artillery strikes.

The installed thermal imaging system is mounted on a gyro-stabilized platform, which allows for accurate tracking of high-speed targets even while on the move. The system is fully digital: the video stream from one camera is used both for target acquisition and for homing in on its own 9M311 anti-aircraft missiles, ensuring a seamless "sensor-strike" cycle. Digital algorithms have also improved the system's resistance to false thermal interference.

The presence of a mixed gun-missile armament (two 30-mm automatic cannons 2A38M and missiles) provides a layered air defense and gives the Tunguska-M1 unique tactical advantages over other SHORAD systems:

In comparison with the Pantsir-S1 air defense system: The Tunguska's tracked chassis was originally designed for direct support of armored columns in rugged terrain, while the wheeled Pantsir is more often used for defending stationary objects in the rear.

In comparison with the Tor-M2 missile system: The Tor is an exclusively missile system. The presence of guns on the Tunguska, however, allows it to destroy cheap drones at close range without wasting expensive missiles.

The deployment of such systems indicates a desire to increase the density of air defense on the front line by integrating modern passive sensors into existing Soviet platforms, which effectively solves the problem of the cost of interception in the face of mass use of drones.
